source: Jansson & Smith (1991) Design fixation. Design Studies 12(1):3-11
finding: Founding paper. Four experiments. A treatment group got a design problem plus a picture of an example solution; a control group got the problem alone. Treatment groups copied features of the example.
numbers: Second-hand only (from Wadinambiarachchi 2024 and Neroni 2017, both opened). Exact N and copy counts not read this session.
quote: a blind adherence to a set of ideas or concepts limiting the output of conceptual design
limits: Paper itself not opened (paywalled; publisher and core.ac.uk pages blocked). Pull the numbers from the paper before citing them.
agent_relevance: S3 fresh contexts: a shown example is the cause. Keep it out of the context that generates ideas.

source: Jansson & Smith (1991) Design fixation. Design Studies 12(1):3-11 (tasks)
finding: Tasks were a car-mounted bicycle rack, a measuring cup for the blind, and a disposable spill-proof coffee cup. Example pictures contained deliberate flaws (features that contradicted the brief).
numbers: Tasks named in Neroni 2017 (opened). No N read.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Test paradigm for our agent: plant a flawed example in the prompt and count how many flaws are copied.

source: Jansson & Smith (1991) Design fixation. Design Studies 12(1):3-11 (warning instruction)
finding: Copying persisted even when participants were told to avoid the example's problem features. So fixation is not a matter of effort or intent.
numbers: Described in Neroni 2017 (opened); no numbers read.
limits: Second-hand. Chrysikou & Weisberg 2005 and Linsey 2010 tested what else reduces it; neither opened.
agent_relevance: G1/S3: a line saying 'do not copy' is weak. Removing the example works better than warning against it.

source: Jansson & Smith (1991) Design fixation. Design Studies 12(1):3-11 (output measures)
finding: Both groups produced a similar number of designs, but treatment groups' designs were more similar to the example. In a later experiment flexibility and originality were lower in the fixation group.
numbers: Per Wadinambiarachchi 2024 (opened): similar counts, more similarity to the example. No figures read.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Fixation shows up as lost variety, not lost quantity. Count distinct categories, not the number of ideas.

source: Chrysikou & Weisberg (2005) Following the wrong footsteps: fixation effects of pictorial examples in a design problem-solving task. JEP:LMC 31(5):1134-1148
finding: Extension of the Jansson-Smith paradigm. Widely cited (322 on Semantic Scholar, 162 on Crossref). Tests example copying and whether instructions to avoid the flaws help.
numbers: Citation counts only. Experiment N and copy counts NOT read (paper paywalled; the only open PDF link was a dead host).
limits: Not opened. Treat as a lead, not as evidence.
agent_relevance: Check its defixation results before designing any 'avoid the example' warning for the agent.

source: Purcell & Gero (1996) Design and other types of fixation. Design Studies 17(4):363-383
finding: Places design fixation among other fixation types. Crossref confirms the record; content not read.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Boundary conditions matter: test fixation per task type rather than assume it.

source: Fixation effects: do they exist in design problem solving? (1993) Environment and Planning B 20
finding: Title asks whether fixation effects exist at all. One web-search summary said replication attempts were largely unsuccessful and clear effects appeared only when the designers' discipline and the pictorial example matched the original. Unverified.
numbers: Not read. Only the title was confirmed by Crossref.
limits: Single search summary, unverified. Do not cite without opening the paper.
agent_relevance: Failed-replication lead. Fetch it before claiming the effect is robust.

source: Vasconcelos & Crilly (2016) Inspiration and fixation: questions, methods, findings, and challenges. Design Studies 42
finding: Reviews 25 studies that use the same basic example-exposure design. Finds 14 manipulated variables (properties of the inspiration source and of the design process). Methods and results vary widely.
numbers: 25 studies; 14 variables (from a Semantic Scholar summary of the abstract).
limits: Abstract-level only; full text blocked (403).
agent_relevance: The literature is heterogeneous. Expect our own agent results to vary with task and example type.

source: Sio, Kotovsky & Cagan (2015) Fixation or inspiration? A meta-analytic review of the role of examples on design processes. Design Studies 39
finding: The standard meta-analysis of example effects in design (title: fixation or inspiration). Content not read.
numbers: Only citation counts (177 Crossref, 203 Semantic Scholar). Effect sizes NOT read; abstract not retrieved.
limits: Not opened. Highest priority for a deeper pass.
agent_relevance: This is the source that would tell us when an example helps. Needed for G8/S3 design.

source: Neroni, Vasconcelos & Crilly (2017) Studying design fixation with a computer-based task. ICED17 vol 8
finding: Mental-set version of design fixation, modelled on Luchins's water jars. Participants designed truss bridges in a game. The group that first met five single-approach trials, then dual-approach trials, kept using the costlier approach.
numbers: 40 recruited, 36 analysed (18 per group). Dual-approach trials solved the costly way: 83% of experimental participants vs 44% of control (chi2(1)=5.90, p=.01); 47% vs 18% of trials (chi2(1)=13.93). Total bridge cost M=$30,077 vs $27,461, t(34)=3.3, d=1.10.
limits: Engineering students, one game, no example given by the experimenter. The fixating solution came from the participants' own earlier work.
agent_relevance: Fixation is not only caused by outside examples. The agent's own first attempt can fixate it. A fresh context removes the carry-over.

source: Neroni, Vasconcelos & Crilly (2017) Studying design fixation with a computer-based task. ICED17 vol 8 (process)
finding: The fixated group spent longer and used more parts, and their first tested design was costlier. The control group started cheap and strengthened.
numbers: Time per trial M=102.5s vs 74.4s, d=.70. Elements M=26.5 vs 19.6, d=.85. First design cost t(34)=3.18, d=1.06. Design-test cycles did not differ (2.44 vs 2.23, p=.45).
limits: Small N. Process measures come from screen recordings of one game.
agent_relevance: Fixation costs effort without more iterations. Track cost per attempt, not only attempt count.

source: Neroni, Vasconcelos & Crilly (2017) Studying design fixation with a computer-based task. ICED17 vol 8 (awareness)
finding: Fixated people often knew they were on autopilot: 9 of 18 (50%) experimental vs 2 of 18 (11%) control said they designed in an automatic way.
numbers: chi2(1)=7.34, p=.007. 23 of 36 (64%) could not guess the study aim; those who guessed were mostly the most stuck.
limits: Self-report after the task.
agent_relevance: Self-report of being stuck arrives too late. Use code signals (repeated structure) instead (G1).

source: Neroni, Vasconcelos & Crilly (2017) Studying design fixation with a computer-based task. ICED17 vol 8 (framing)
finding: Gives the history: design fixation comes from functional fixedness (Duncker 1945) and Einstellung or mental set (Luchins 1942). Argues design fixation is closer to mental set. Notes the field relies on subjective metrics and open-ended tasks.
numbers: Luchins: most participants kept a long pouring sequence when a one-step solution existed; a control group given only the extinction problem solved it quickly.
limits: Summary of other studies.
agent_relevance: Two mechanisms for our agent: example-driven and self-generated set. Both need handling.

source: Howard et al. (2013) Applying the neuroscience of creativity to creativity training. Front Hum Neurosci 7:656
finding: Reused the three Jansson-Smith tasks (flawed examples) before and after a lecture on how the brain makes associations. Fixation elements dropped after training.
numbers: 12 teams of 4 engineering students, no control group. Before: 86 designs (7.2/team), 76 fixation elements, ratio 0.88. After: 89 designs (7.4/team), 48 elements, ratio 0.53, p=.026.
limits: No control, practice effect not ruled out, teams told to avoid the flaws. Read through a page-summary tool, not the PDF.
agent_relevance: Awareness training reduced copying in humans. The LLM analogue is an instruction, but G1 says doubt only on a signal.

source: Howard et al. (2013) (mechanism claim)
finding: Explains fixation by associative networks and lateral inhibition: familiar, typical examples activate related concepts and suppress distant ones. Fixation grows the longer one works on a problem.
numbers: No new data for this claim.
quote: Fixation occurs more often with examples that are typical and familiar in respect to a designer's background
limits: Authors' account; not tested directly.
agent_relevance: Matches the autoregressive story in a24. A long context on one idea raises fixation risk, which supports fresh contexts.

source: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou & Velloso (2024) The effects of generative AI on design fixation and divergent thinking. CHI 2024
finding: Between-participants test in the Jansson-Smith style: all got a brief plus an example chatbot avatar, then no help, Google image search, or Midjourney. AI images raised fixation on the example and cut fluency, variety and originality.
numbers: N=60 novices, 20 min. Fixation = shared features out of 14. GenAI +0.32 (89% CI .11 to .55, BF 124); image search +0.27 (CI .05 to .49, BF 42). Fluency total effect: GenAI CI -0.7 to 0.28 (BF 3.2, 76% prob. negative), image search -0.49 (CI -0.9 to -0.10, BF 46.6). Variety: GenAI -0.29 (BF 5.9), image search -0.40 (BF 11.4). Originality GenAI -0.03 (97% prob. negative).
limits: Bayesian models; some intervals cross zero; AI users spent time prompting, so fluency fell partly through time. Short task, novices, one brief.
agent_relevance: Showing a finished idea is itself an example. The agent should not see another model's finished idea before it generates its own.

source: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou & Velloso (2024) The effects of generative AI on design fixation and divergent thinking. CHI 2024 (copy behaviour)
finding: Qualitative: many participants copied then tweaked an AI image. Some showed 'fixation displacement': they fixated on a prompt-led image that scored low on the shared-features count.
numbers: Participant quote: 'I would just kind of copy it and then tweak'.
limits: Interview data from 60 participants. The count metric misses displaced fixation.
agent_relevance: A feature-count detector will miss second-order fixation. Add a semantic-distance check.

source: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou & Velloso (2024) The effects of generative AI on design fixation and divergent thinking. CHI 2024 (restating the 1991 design)
finding: Gives a clear secondary description of Jansson & Smith: four experiments, treatment vs control, similar counts, fixation group's ideas more similar to the example, lower flexibility and originality.
numbers: Basis for a01 and a04, the only available description of the original results.
limits: Second-hand description.
agent_relevance: Bounds what we know of the original paper.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Understanding design fixation in generative AI. arXiv 2502.05870
finding: Proposes that GenAI itself shows design fixation, with a definition, causes (training data, prompts, context) and manifestations in text and image models. Evidence is mostly qualitative.
numbers: 10 novice participants (aged 20 to 26) designed a chair with GenAI. Proportion of unique terms: ChatGPT output 67.4% vs 78.2% for human Red Dot texts.
limits: N=10, no control group. Small term-diversity comparison.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. Hypothesis source only; stronger LLM tests are Deng 2026 and Meincke 2024.

source: Deng, Brucks & Toubia (2026) Examining and addressing barriers to diversity in LLM-generated ideas. arXiv 2602.20408
finding: Direct test of fixation in an LLM. Within one session of 10 sequential product ideas, GPT-4o accumulates idea categories at the same rate as humans. LLMs fixate about as much as people, far below the possible maximum.
numbers: 99 humans vs 99 simulated GPT-4o participants, 10 ideas each. Slope of category accumulation: human 1.035, LLM 1.013 (p=.51); maximum 3.0. Unique categories 12.68 vs 12.46 (p=.45).
limits: One model (gpt-4o-2024-11-20), one task (fitness product ideas), categories labelled by GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: The agent fixates inside one long context at human levels. Strong support for S3 fresh contexts.

source: Deng, Brucks & Toubia (2026) Examining and addressing barriers to diversity in LLM-generated ideas. arXiv 2602.20408 (first ideas)
finding: The collective gap between LLMs and humans is not from fixation but from missing knowledge partitioning: first ideas across LLM sessions overlap far more.
numbers: First-idea categories (groups of 10): human 14.51 vs LLM 8.37; combinations 9.17 vs 5.88; pairwise distance 2.41 vs 1.51 (all p<.001).
limits: Same limits as a20.
agent_relevance: Samples from one model are not independent (G4). Fresh contexts fix within-run fixation only; spread across samples needs other levers.

source: Deng, Brucks & Toubia (2026) Examining and addressing barriers to diversity in LLM-generated ideas. arXiv 2602.20408 (seeding)
finding: Giving each LLM a human first idea as a seed did not raise fixation; seeded LLMs had slightly steeper slopes than default.
numbers: Seeded slope 1.063 vs default 1.013 vs human 1.035 (seeded vs human p=.42).
limits: One seed idea; not the Jansson-Smith flawed-example design.
agent_relevance: One neutral seed is not a flawed example. Do not assume seeding is harmful.

source: Deng, Brucks & Toubia (2026) Examining and addressing barriers to diversity in LLM-generated ideas. arXiv 2602.20408 (chain of thought)
finding: Chain-of-thought (draft short summaries, then revise to be bolder) cut fixation in LLMs but did nothing for humans. CoT with ordinary personas beat humans.
numbers: LLM slope 1.013 to 1.363 with CoT (p<.001); persona 0.876 to 1.086. Human 1.035 vs 1.035 with CoT (p=.997). Persona + CoT exceeded humans by 26%.
limits: Persona alone raised fixation (slope .876). GPT-4o only. Diversity labels by an LLM.
agent_relevance: Draft-then-revise is a candidate operator only if it wins at equal tokens (G7). Persona voters conflict with G4.

source: Deng, Brucks & Toubia (2026) Examining and addressing barriers to diversity in LLM-generated ideas. arXiv 2602.20408 (theory)
finding: Carries two human mechanisms over to LLMs: part-list cueing (initial activation inhibits related concepts) and unconscious plagiarism (examples leak features even when told to avoid them, Marsh et al. 1999). Autoregressive decoding is the proposed LLM analogue.
numbers: Cited human anchors (not read): Dahl & Moreau 2002, Smith et al. 1993, Bayus 2013, Dane 2010.
limits: Theory by analogy, cited second-hand.
agent_relevance: Part-list cueing predicts that listing prior ideas in the prompt blocks new ones.

source: Meincke, Mollick & Terwiesch (2024) Prompting diverse ideas: increasing AI idea variance. arXiv 2402.01727
finding: GPT-4 idea pools are less diverse than human pools; prompt choice changes this. 35 prompts compared on cosine similarity, unique ideas and speed of exhaustion. Chain-of-thought came closest to humans.
numbers: Cosine similarity: human groups 0.243; GPT-4 prompts 0.255 to 0.432; baseline about 0.377; Steve Jobs persona 0.368. Unique ideas about 3700 (base) vs about 4700 (CoT).
limits: One domain (college-student products under $50), GPT-4 only, working paper.
agent_relevance: Same finding as Deng 2026 from another direction: CoT reduces repetition. The idea space exhausts, so stop sampling the same prompt.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? arXiv 2409.04109
finding: LLMs repeat themselves when they overgenerate. Of 4000 seed ideas per topic, only about 200 were non-duplicates (cosine > 0.8 counted as duplicate). LLM ideas were still rated more novel than human ideas.
numbers: Novelty mean AI 5.64, AI + human rerank 5.81, human 4.84 (p<.01). 49 expert idea writers, 79 reviewers.
limits: Dedup used MiniLM embeddings; ratings by experts; the paper also finds LLMs unreliable as evaluators.
agent_relevance: Repeated sampling from one prompt saturates. Fresh contexts alone are not enough; vary the prompt or add a conditioned stage.

source: Doshi & Hauser (2024) Generative AI enhances creativity but reduces the diversity of novel content. arXiv 2312.00506
finding: Showing GPT-4 story ideas to writers raised rated novelty and usefulness but made stories more similar to the AI idea and to each other: an anchoring effect.
numbers: 293 writers (Human only, 1 AI idea, up to 5 AI ideas); 600 evaluators. Novelty +6.7% (b=.259, p=.001); 5 ideas +8.1%. Similarity to the AI idea +5.2% (b=4.29, p<.001) with 1 idea. Similarity to other stories b=.871 (1 idea), .718 (5 ideas).
limits: Short 8-sentence stories; writers' own ratings showed no difference; gains largest for less creative writers.
agent_relevance: Example effects cut both ways: individual quality up, diversity down. An example can help one run and hurt a population of runs.

source: Anderson, Shah & Kreminski (2024) Homogenization effects of LLMs on human creative ideation. C&C '24; arXiv 2402.01536
finding: ChatGPT users produced ideas more alike across people (group level) but not more alike within a person. Homogenisation came from shared suggestions, not extra individual fixation.
numbers: 36 participants, 1271 ideas, TTCT tasks. Group-level divergence ChatGPT M=.24 (SD .07) vs Oblique Strategies M=.28 (SD .08), t(32)=2.154, p=.03. Individual level no difference. Flexibility 8.58 vs 6.77 categories (p=.001, d=.54); fluency and elaboration also higher with ChatGPT.
limits: Within-subject; small N; best embedding agreed with human coders only 59%.
agent_relevance: Separates individual fixation from collective sameness, as Deng 2026 does. Treat them as two problems.

source: Using design strategies from microfluidic device patents to support idea generation (2018) Microfluidics and Nanofluidics
finding: Strategy cards for idea generation. No fixation control, so it does not test fixation. Mentions fixation only as attachment to early ideas (citing Cross 2001, Ball 1994, Jansson & Smith 1991).
numbers: 14 researchers; 45 concepts without strategies (3.2 each) vs 40 with (2.9 each). Participants rated strategy-aided sets more creative, unique and diverse.
limits: No example-vs-no-example control; self-rating; chi-squared reported without values.
agent_relevance: Card-style defixation exists but is untested for fixation. Low weight.
